Extinction Bursts.short_definition: A sudden, sharper surge of a pressure tactic right after it stops working, as the person tries harder to get the old result back.
Extinction Bursts.core_meaning: A sudden, sharper surge of a pressure tactic right after it stops working, as the person tries harder to get the old result back.
Extinction Bursts.expanded_definition: The term comes from behavior science: when a habit that used to pay off stops paying off, it often gets louder before it fades. In relationships, this can look like more messages, more anger or bigger promises right after you hold a limit for the first time. A spike after a new boundary can come from hurt or shock and does not show what anyone meant. It becomes a pattern when each limit you hold is met with something heavier than before.
Extinction Bursts.plain_language_summary: You hold a limit for the first time, and things suddenly get worse, not better. The pressure that used to work gets turned up because it stopped working.
Extinction Bursts.why_this_matters: The first boundary that actually works is the one that costs the most. It can teach you that holding a limit makes things worse, so giving in starts to feel like the only way to get peace again.
what_it_is: A jump in volume, frequency or intensity that begins right after you refuse or hold a line, not before.
The same method as before, only louder: forty messages instead of four, or a longer silent treatment, or a bigger display of hurt.
Sometimes a brand-new method appears, such as guilt where there had been anger, once the old one stops working.
A shape that is only visible in time order: what happened, what you did differently, and what came next.
what_it_sounds_like: "You've never done this to me before. What has gotten into you?"
Eleven missed calls and a stream of texts the evening after you said no to a request.
"Fine. If that's how you feel, I'll just stop trying. Is that what you want?"
A cold week of silence that suddenly flips into flowers, tears and a long apology on day eight.
"I can't believe you'd do this after everything."
A family group chat that fills with messages about you a day after you declined the usual favor.
A coworker who used to ask once and now copies your manager after you said you could not take the extra shift.
what_it_is_not: Hurt or panic after a surprising boundary. Most people react badly to a change in a long-standing arrangement and then settle.
A person who is upset, says so once, and then adjusts over the next few weeks.
Honest persistence about something urgent, such as a bill that really is due, which is not tied to your having said no.
Grief or fear in someone who is already struggling, where the intensity comes from their situation and not from the old method failing.
Your own wish to find a pattern in a rough week. A bad few days after a hard talk is not yet a shape.
this_may_be_it_when: The worsening starts within hours or days of your holding a line and not before.
The new behavior is clearly bigger than anything you saw while you were still going along.
The pressure falls away the moment you give in, and returns when you do not.
Each time you hold a limit, the response is heavier than the last.
The demand itself never changes; only the force behind it does.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The reaction peaks in the first few days and then settles, even though you have not given in.
They name their feelings and ask for time, and do not increase contact or demands.
Your boundary changed something large in their life, and the upset is about that change.
They accept the limit on some points while grieving it, and do not test it again.
The surge also appears in places unrelated to your refusal, which points to something else going on for them.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Shock. A person who has never heard you say no may need a few days to take it in.
Fear of losing something that matters to them, expressed clumsily and loudly.
A bad stretch in their own life that happens to land on the same week as your boundary.
common_false_positives: A child testing a new bedtime rule for a week, which is normal learning and not manipulation.
A friend who sends several worried texts because you went quiet after a hard day.
A landlord or lender chasing a real deadline more urgently because the first notice went unanswered.
discernment_questions: Did the increase begin after I held a line, or was it already building before?
Does it ease when I give in and return when I do not?
Is the new behavior the same method turned up, or a different one that appeared when the first stopped working?
Over several weeks, is the response to my limits getting softer, or heavier?
Would I describe this as upset about the change, or as an effort to reverse it?
less_concerning_if: The strongest reaction comes in the first days and then eases while the boundary stays in place.
They can say, even awkwardly, that they are struggling with the change and still respect it.
Others who have set limits with them report a similar short adjustment that passed.
more_concerning_if: The surge includes threats, showing up uninvited, following you, or pressure on your children, income or housing.
Each new limit gets a worse reaction than the one before.
Third parties are pulled in to lean on you after you said no.
pattern_over_time_signs: You start to dread holding a limit because you remember the week that followed the last one.
The gap between your refusal and the heavy reaction shortens.
You find yourself giving in earlier each time to avoid the surge.
Good stretches follow only when you have given way, which teaches you what each choice costs.
Extinction Bursts.repair_check: Once you have named the surge, watch what happens to the limit itself. Repair looks like the surge ending while the boundary stays in place, and an acknowledgment that the escalation was too much. A calm week bought by your quietly dropping the limit is a return of the old arrangement.
Extinction Bursts.boundary_respect_check: Compare the first refusal with the fourth. When a limit is respected, the answer to it gets quieter each time, even if the disappointment remains. When the answer keeps getting louder, the limit is being treated as a problem to be overcome.
Extinction Bursts.psychological_mechanism: When a behavior has paid off before, it tends to be repeated harder before it is dropped. On the receiving end, relief when the surge stops can strengthen the habit of yielding. Escalation also tends to feel like proof that you were wrong to refuse, since the discomfort arrives immediately and the benefit of the limit arrives later.
Extinction Bursts.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe doubting a boundary that was reasonable, replaying the moment before the surge, and feeling guilty for the fallout. Some describe giving in just to end the noise, and then feeling angry at themselves. Others say that naming this shape gave them the nerve to hold the second limit.

response_options.soft_clarification: Describe the sequence once, without blame: 'I noticed that after I said no, the messages went from a few a day to dozens. Can we talk about what is going on?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold the same limit and shorten your replies. Repeating one calm sentence is enough: 'My answer is the same as yesterday.'
response_options.disengagement: Mute the thread and answer only at set times, such as once in the evening. Let the volume pass without chasing it.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend before you hold the limit, so someone knows what to expect and can check in the day after, when the surge tends to peak.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Keep every message after your refusal and reply in writing with one line. If the pressure keeps rising, give the thread to a manager or HR.

Extinction Bursts.boundary_script: "My answer has not changed, and I understand you are upset. I will reply to messages once this evening. Please do not call again before then."
Extinction Bursts.safety_note: A surge after a boundary is not dangerous in every case. It becomes a safety matter if it includes threats, turning up at your home or work, tracking you, or contact with your kids or employer. Keep dated copies, and talk to a domestic violence advocate or someone you trust before you decide how to proceed.
misuse_warning: Calling a person's hurt reaction an 'extinction burst' can dismiss real feelings about a change that did affect them.
Treating every spike of anger as a tactic can turn a normal adjustment period into an accusation.
Extinction Bursts.how_to_distinguish_from_related: An Ultimatum sets a fixed deadline with a stated cost; a burst has no new demand, only more force behind the old one. Urgency Manufacturing invents time pressure from the start, while a burst appears only after resistance. False Dilemma narrows your choices to two; a burst may offer no choices at all, just rising volume until you give way.

Door-in-the-Face.short_definition: Making a big request that is likely to be refused so that the smaller request that follows seems modest and hard to turn down.
Door-in-the-Face.core_meaning: Making a big request that is likely to be refused so that the smaller request that follows seems modest and hard to turn down.
Door-in-the-Face.expanded_definition: The name comes from a salesman slamming a door: the first ask is expected to get a no. The second, smaller ask is the one that was wanted all along. Agreeing to it can feel like returning a favor, because the other person seems to have backed down. Plenty of honest bargaining works this way, so one round proves nothing. It is a pattern when the big ask is never really meant and the same two-step shows up again and again.
Door-in-the-Face.plain_language_summary: Someone asks for far too much, you say no, and then they ask for less. The smaller request feels like a favor to them, so it is hard to refuse.
Door-in-the-Face.why_this_matters: Relief at the smaller ask stands in for judging it. The second request gets measured against the first, not against what is fair, and a yes given to feel gracious can leave you carrying more than you chose.
what_it_is: A two-step request: an oversized ask, then a reduced one soon after your refusal.
The reduction is framed as a concession, as though a favor were being granted to you.
Common with fundraising, sales, favors between relatives and workplace volunteering.
Powered by the urge to match a concession with one of your own, which is what makes the smaller ask hard to decline.
what_it_sounds_like: "Could you take the whole month of shifts? No? Okay, then how about just next weekend?"
"Would you lend me ten thousand? That's too much, I get it. Could you do two?"
"I met you halfway, so now it's your turn to meet me."
"Fine, forget the donation. Surely you can sign up for the monthly plan?"
"I was going to ask you to move in for a year, but a few weeks would be okay."
"I came down a lot. The least you can do is say yes to this."
what_it_is_not: Ordinary negotiation, where both sides know the opening position is high and expect to settle in the middle.
Someone who truly wanted the larger thing, asked for it, and then settled for less in good faith.
A person who learns your limits from your first answer and then asks for something that fits them.
Two separate requests that happen to arrive close together.
A reasonable request that you find uncomfortable only because it follows a stressful one.
this_may_be_it_when: The first request was so extreme that no one could have expected a yes.
The smaller request comes within minutes or days, and is presented as a concession you now owe something for.
You notice the same big-then-small order in several separate dealings with this person.
The smaller ask would have seemed too much if it had been the first thing said.
They draw attention to how much they came down, instead of explaining why they need the thing.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The first ask matched a real need, and they scaled it back after hearing your constraints.
They accept no to the smaller ask as easily as to the larger one.
They tell you plainly what they are really after and what the minimum would be.
There is no talk of what you owe in return for their flexibility.
The sequence happened once and has not repeated.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often ask for the ideal and then adjust once they hear what is realistic.
A person unsure what you can give may start high just to find out.
A team asking for a big budget may expect to receive part of it.
common_false_positives: A haggle at a market, where both sides expect it.
A charity that offers a lower-cost option to people who cannot afford the main program.
A relative who asks for a whole weekend of help, hears you are busy, and then happily takes an hour.
discernment_questions: Would I consider the smaller request fair if it had been the first thing they asked?
Do I feel I owe them because they came down?
Has the same big-then-small order happened before?
Did they ask what I could do, or go straight to a lower number of their own?
What is the actual size of this request without the first one beside it?
less_concerning_if: The smaller request is something you would have been glad to do if asked first.
They are as content with a no on either request.
They explain why the first ask was so large, in terms that make sense.
more_concerning_if: The small ask involves your money, housing, legal paperwork or access to your accounts.
A refusal of the big ask is followed by hurt or anger, and the small ask then arrives as the way back to their good graces.
The big ask always seems designed to fail.
pattern_over_time_signs: You catch yourself saying yes to the second ask without any thought, because the first one made it feel light.
You begin bracing for the huge ask as the opening of a routine.
The 'small' asks add up to far more than you would ever have agreed to in one go.
You feel more indebted to this person than the facts support.
Door-in-the-Face.repair_check: Ask what happens when you go back and say you will reconsider the smaller request. Honest acknowledgment sounds like 'you're right, I made it harder to say no.' A repeat of the sequence next month, with the same pair of asks, shows nothing has changed.
Door-in-the-Face.boundary_respect_check: Try declining both requests and see how the conversation goes. If a clean no to the second ask is received calmly, the first ask was probably just an opening position. If the second no brings guilt about their concession, that is informative.
Door-in-the-Face.psychological_mechanism: People tend to feel they should answer a concession with a concession. A smaller request after a refusal can read as a step toward you, so saying yes feels like fairness. The first, extreme ask also changes the reference point, which can make a moderate request feel light even if it is not.
Door-in-the-Face.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe agreeing and then feeling oddly cornered, as if a yes had been taken out of them. Some say they could not work out what had bothered them until they separated the second request from the first. Others mention resentment toward a favor that felt requested and also owed.

response_options.soft_clarification: Pull the smaller request apart from the first: 'Forget the first ask for a second. On its own, this one is bigger than I can do.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline without trading: 'I did not say no to the first one to get a better deal on the second. My answer to both is no.'
response_options.disengagement: Do not answer straight away. Say you will get back to them tomorrow, and use the gap to look at the second ask alone.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone you trust both requests in order and ask what they would say to the second if it had come first.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask for the request in writing with the actual scope and deadline, so the small version is judged on its own terms and not against the big one.

Door-in-the-Face.boundary_script: "I see you have scaled it down, and I appreciate that. Taken on its own, it is still more than I can take on, so my answer is no. I would be glad to help with something smaller than this."
Door-in-the-Face.safety_note: On its own this is a pressure tactic about requests, not a danger signal. It would raise concern if the asks involve money, signing papers, access to your accounts or your home, or if a refusal brings threats. In those cases, take time before agreeing and talk to someone independent, such as a legal aid clinic or a financial counselor.
misuse_warning: Calling normal bargaining 'door-in-the-face' can make you suspicious of every negotiation, including honest ones.
Using the label to dismiss a real, reduced request can leave a person without help they genuinely needed.
Door-in-the-Face.how_to_distinguish_from_related: A False Dilemma shrinks your choices to two and treats both as costly; the door-in-the-face first ask is simply meant to be refused, so the second feels light. Urgency Manufacturing works through a clock, while this works through your sense that a concession deserves one in return. Sunk Cost Exploitation leans on what you have already put in, and here you have put in nothing until the second yes.

Anchoring.short_definition: Putting forward a first number, price or claim that then shapes how every later figure and offer is judged.
Anchoring.core_meaning: Putting forward a first number, price or claim that then shapes how every later figure and offer is judged.
Anchoring.expanded_definition: People tend to judge a value by comparing it to the first one they hear, even when the first one is arbitrary. A seller names a high price, a manager names a salary band, a relative says how much you 'usually' give. Everything after is measured against that figure. Stating an opening number is normal in any negotiation. It becomes a tactic when the number has no basis and is used to make a worse offer look generous.
Anchoring.plain_language_summary: The first number you hear sticks in your mind and makes later numbers look big or small by comparison, even when that first number was made up.
Anchoring.why_this_matters: Everything that follows gets measured against a figure or framing that was never justified, so an offer that would look unreasonable on its own can seem fair, and you may feel you won something when you did not.
what_it_is: An opening price, salary, deadline or amount that sets the range for the whole discussion.
Often a crossed-out 'original' price beside a sale price, or a 'suggested' tip or donation amount.
Works even when people know the first number is arbitrary, which is why it is used in sales, pay talks and settlements.
Different from a real constraint: an anchor is chosen for its effect, not because it reflects cost, rules or facts.
what_it_sounds_like: "The listing price is four hundred, but for you, three-fifty."
"People with your experience usually ask for much more than that." (said before any figure is mentioned)
"We're thinking about forty thousand for this role." (when the going rate is well above)
"Everyone else in the family gave a hundred, but give what you can."
A 'was $199, now $89' tag on an item that was never sold for $199.
"The other side wants a million. I think we can get them down to six hundred thousand."
what_it_is_not: An honest opening position in a bargain, where both sides know the first number is a starting point.
A real price list, rate card or pay scale that states what something costs.
Someone with little experience of pricing blurting out a high number without any strategy behind it.
A reference you picked yourself, such as the price you saw last week at another shop.
Natural comparison: noticing one thing is cheaper than another is just using information.
this_may_be_it_when: A number is said first, with nothing explaining where it comes from.
The figure falls well outside the real range, and later 'concessions' still land above fair.
Questions about where the number came from get a vague answer or a change of subject.
You notice you are bargaining down from their figure and not up from your own.
The same sort of high first figure turns up in a pattern across their dealings with you.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They can show how the number was built, such as costs, comparable sales or a published scale.
They will happily hear your figure first, or ask for it.
The opening figure is close to what the market supports.
It is a standard fixed price and no movement is offered or implied.
They explain the number is a starting point and invite you to counter.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Sellers and employers often start a little high because they expect to move.
A person may genuinely not know what is typical and quote the first figure that comes to mind.
A stated price may reflect costs you cannot see.
common_false_positives: A shop's sticker price in a store that does not haggle.
A friend quoting what they paid for a similar item last year.
A mediator's opening suggestion that both parties are free to reject.
discernment_questions: Where did this first number come from, and can they show me?
If I had heard a different first number, would my view of this offer be different?
Do I know what the typical range is from a source other than them?
Am I judging the deal on its own merits or only against their opening figure?
Would I think the later offer was fair if I had not heard the first one?
less_concerning_if: You can check the figure against independent sources, and it holds up.
They are open to a counteroffer, including one well below theirs.
The first number is labeled plainly as an opening position.
more_concerning_if: The anchored figure involves a settlement, a debt, rent, a wage or legal fees, where a bad outcome is hard to undo.
You are pressed to answer before you can look up the range.
They treat any counter below the anchor as an insult or a sign of bad faith.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your own sense of what something is worth drifts toward their numbers.
You find yourself pleased with deals that, on later checking, were ordinary or poor.
Their first figure keeps being the highest or lowest one in the room.
You start asking for less than you wanted, to stay near the range they set.
Anchoring.repair_check: If you point out that the first number had no basis, a straight answer would be to explain how it was set and to restate the offer from a fair starting point. Quietly lowering it a bit while insisting the first figure was reasonable moves the number without changing the habit.
Anchoring.boundary_respect_check: Try putting your own number on the table before they answer, or ask where theirs came from. Do they engage with the question, or press on as if you had not spoken? Their ease with being challenged tells you most.
Anchoring.psychological_mechanism: People tend to adjust from the first figure they hear, and usually stop adjusting too soon. Even a number known to be random can pull judgments toward it. The pull can be stronger when you are short of information or time, and a later 'discount' can feel like a gain that you earned.
Anchoring.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe agreeing to a price or a pay level and later working out that they had accepted the other side's frame. Some feel foolish when they compare notes with others. Some describe a lingering sense of having been handled, even though nothing false was said.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the source: 'How did you get to that number? I'd like to understand it before I answer.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Reset the frame yourself: 'I'm going to work from my own research on this, not from your opening figure. Here is what I have found.'
response_options.disengagement: Do not respond to the figure straight away. Take a day, look up typical ranges, and return with your own range.
response_options.support_seeking: Ask someone who has bought, sold or been paid in this field what a normal figure is, before you reply.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In pay or contract talks, research the range from published scales or peers first, and state your number before they state theirs if you can.

Anchoring.boundary_script: "Thanks for the opening figure. I would like to see how it was worked out, and I've done my own research on the range. Can we start from what comparable cases show?"
Anchoring.safety_note: A high opening number is a financial pressure, and rarely a danger by itself. It matters more where the stakes are heavy and hard to undo: a legal settlement, a debt payment plan, a lease, or a pay offer tied to your immigration status. For those, get independent advice from legal aid or a financial counselor before you answer.
misuse_warning: Calling every opening price 'anchoring' can make normal negotiation look like manipulation and leave you unable to bargain at all.
Accusing someone of anchoring when they simply quoted a figure they believe in shuts down a fair talk.
Anchoring.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Urgency Manufacturing shortens your time, while anchoring distorts your sense of the figure, however long you take. A False Dilemma limits your choices to two; an anchor leaves your choices open but tilts where you land. Sunk Cost Exploitation uses what you have already spent to keep you in, whereas an anchor works on the very first figure you hear, before you have spent anything.

Emotional Flooding.short_definition: Pouring on emotion so fast and so hard that the other person cannot think, and speed or intensity is mistaken for closeness.
Emotional Flooding.core_meaning: Pouring on emotion so fast and so hard that the other person cannot think, and speed or intensity is mistaken for closeness.
Emotional Flooding.expanded_definition: Flooding is a state of being so emotionally overwhelmed that thinking narrows, and it can happen to anyone in a heated moment. As a tactic, it means keeping someone there on purpose or by habit: back-to-back declarations, crises and reconciliations, with no ordinary days in between. Strong feelings are not a tactic, and many real relationships are intense. The question is whether the intensity leaves you any quiet time in which to judge what is happening.
Emotional Flooding.plain_language_summary: Things move through such big highs and lows, so quickly, that you never get a calm moment to think. The intensity can feel like love, but it also keeps you from seeing clearly.
Emotional Flooding.why_this_matters: Sustained intensity leaves no quiet stretch in which to assess anything. Speed gets mistaken for depth, and there is no calm vantage point from which to notice what you are agreeing to.
what_it_is: A run of big emotional events: declarations, fights, tearful reconciliations, urgent crises, in quick succession.
A shortage of ordinary time: no flat, boring, restful days when you could step back.
Often runs along with fast commitment, such as talk of forever within weeks.
Different from one overwhelming conversation: it is the sustained pace that matters.
what_it_sounds_like: "I've never felt this way about anyone. I know you're the one." (said in the first week)
"I can't breathe when you're not here. Please don't leave me tonight."
A midnight fight, a dawn apology and a gift by noon, repeated most weeks.
"If you really cared, you would have dropped everything."
"I'm in pieces. I need you to fix this right now."
Dozens of long, intense messages a day, swinging between adoration and despair.
what_it_is_not: The early excitement of a new relationship, which can be intense and then settle into something steadier.
A person in a real crisis, such as a death or job loss, who is overwhelmed because the situation is.
A naturally expressive person whose feelings are big and quickly shown, with nothing engineered behind it.
A single heated argument that left both of you shaken.
Your own flooding in a hard talk. Anyone's thinking narrows when they are overwhelmed.
this_may_be_it_when: You cannot remember the last ordinary, quiet day together.
Big declarations or commitments arrive faster than you have had time to get to know the person.
Every attempt to slow down is met with hurt, panic or a new crisis.
You often make decisions, such as moving in or sending money, in the middle of an emotional peak.
You feel exhausted, as well as swept up.
this_may_not_be_it_when: There are calm stretches, and the relationship is fine in them.
Slowing down, when you ask, is accepted without punishment.
The intensity matches something real going on in their life and eases when it passes.
Decisions are made on ordinary days and not only at emotional peaks.
You feel energized and clear-headed in the relationship, and not drained.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: New love can feel overwhelming to both people at once.
Someone with a history of stormy relationships may know no other pace and not intend any pressure.
Grief, illness or loss can fill a relationship with intense feelings for a while.
common_false_positives: A vacation romance or the first month of dating, where both people are swept up.
A friendship in which one person is going through a divorce and needs a great deal of support.
A family reunion that is emotional from beginning to end.
discernment_questions: When did we last have an ordinary, quiet stretch together?
Do I make big choices when I am calm, or when I am at an emotional peak?
Can I ask to go slower without causing a storm?
Do I feel more like myself or less in the calm moments?
Would my closest friend say this pace looks right for how long we have known each other?
less_concerning_if: There are real calm stretches, and you enjoy them.
You can slow things down without being punished for it.
The intensity belongs to a clear, passing event.
more_concerning_if: Big commitments, money or moving in are pressed through at the peak of an emotional episode.
You are cut off from friends and family during the whirlwind.
Every pause you ask for is answered with a crisis or a threat of self-harm.
pattern_over_time_signs: You cannot recall what you actually like about the person when things are calm.
You are sleeping less, and your friends have seen less of you.
You feel constant relief when a storm passes, and dread when it is quiet.
The highs are what you stay for and the lows are what you apologize for.
Emotional Flooding.repair_check: Repair in this case shows up as the pace itself changing: ordinary days appear, and a request to slow down is met with agreement and not a new crisis. A moving apology in the middle of another peak does not change the rhythm.
Emotional Flooding.boundary_respect_check: A quiet evening alone is a small test. Someone who respects the request lets it be quiet, even if disappointed. If the temperature rises the moment you ask for calm, or a fresh crisis lands at your door, the request itself is being met with more flooding.
Emotional Flooding.psychological_mechanism: When feelings run very high, thinking tends to narrow and people lean on gut sense and the wish to end the discomfort. Strong highs followed by relief can feel like deep bonding, and a sense of urgency can be read as proof of love. Without calm stretches, there may be few chances to compare what is said with what is done.
Emotional Flooding.possible_impact_on_receiver: Whirlwind relationships are often remembered as exhausting and thrilling in the same breath. Some report poor sleep, lost touch with friends and a fog about what they actually wanted. Some say they only saw the pace once they had a quiet month for the first time.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name the pace without blame: 'I care about you, and I am worn out. I would like to try a few ordinary days.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Defer big decisions: 'I don't make decisions like this in the middle of a hard night. We can talk about it on Saturday.'
response_options.disengagement: When the intensity peaks, say you need to sleep on it and leave the conversation until morning.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend you trust about the last month, day by day, and ask whether the pace looks right from the outside.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager or client sets a constant crisis tone, ask for requests in writing and respond within a set window, not in the moment.

Emotional Flooding.boundary_script: "I do care, and I'm too tired to think clearly tonight. I'm going to sleep, and we can talk through this properly tomorrow afternoon."
Emotional Flooding.safety_note: Intensity alone is not an emergency. Pay attention if the whirlwind comes with threats of self-harm if you step back, or pressure to move in or hand over money. Cutting off your friends, or any physical fear, matters too. Then reach out to a trusted person, and consider a domestic violence advocate or a crisis line, depending on what you are facing.
misuse_warning: Calling a passionate new relationship 'flooding' can make real, mutual excitement look suspicious.
Using the word to describe a person's real distress can dismiss someone who is struggling.
Emotional Flooding.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Urgency Manufacturing is about time: a deadline you are given. Flooding is about feeling: a pace of emotion that leaves no space. An Ultimatum is a single hard choice with a penalty attached, while flooding is a sustained atmosphere with no clear demand. Interrogation demands justification from you, and flooding mostly offers you emotion to respond to.

Cognitive Overload.short_definition: Burying someone in more information, steps or demands than they can take in, so they cannot judge a decision clearly.
Cognitive Overload.core_meaning: Burying someone in more information, steps or demands than they can take in, so they cannot judge a decision clearly.
Cognitive Overload.expanded_definition: Everyone can only hold so much in mind at once. Past that point, people skim, guess, or agree just to be done. Cognitive overload as a tactic means a decision arrives wrapped in a flood of detail, jargon, paperwork or competing demands, often with a deadline. Complicated things are often truly complicated, so the amount alone proves nothing. What matters is whether the volume is needed, and what happens when you ask for less.
Cognitive Overload.plain_language_summary: You are handed so much to read, learn or do at once that you cannot think straight, and saying yes becomes the quickest way out.
Cognitive Overload.why_this_matters: Agreement becomes the fastest way out of the overwhelm, so the decision that results was never really weighed, and you may find later that you consented to things you did not understand.
what_it_is: A heavy dose of detail, terms or tasks delivered right before a decision is needed.
Pages of small print, a long list of changes, or many people asking for different things at once.
Requests for time met with more material, and not with a pause.
Found in contracts, medical or insurance paperwork, workplace changes, and arguments where ten complaints arrive in one go.
what_it_sounds_like: A forty-page agreement handed over at the signing table with 'it's all standard, just initial here.'
"There are twelve things I need to go through with you, and we are going to do them all tonight."
"I've sent you the whole file, and I need your answer by the morning."
"Do you want me to explain the policy? It will take an hour, and most people just sign."
A long email with seven different questions and a note that all must be answered today.
"If you had read the terms, you would know this."
what_it_is_not: A decision that is truly complex, such as a mortgage or a medical consent, which does need a lot of real information.
An anxious person who explains everything because they want to be thorough, with no wish to hurry you.
A busy period at work when many real tasks pile up, with nobody designing it.
Plain jargon from someone who forgot you are not an expert in their field.
Your own tiredness or stress, which lowers how much you can take in on any day.
this_may_be_it_when: The amount of material is out of proportion to the choice, and a deadline hangs over it.
Asking for a summary or more time produces more material.
Key terms sit deep in the pile where they are easy to miss.
You are made to feel slow or difficult for needing to read it.
The same person has used volume to wear you down on earlier decisions.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They offer a short summary, and also give you the full version if you want it.
You are given real time, and your questions are answered plainly.
The deadline is set by an outside body, such as a court or a benefits office, and not by them.
The extra detail is mostly there to protect you, such as listing risks.
They are willing to slow down when you ask.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A professional who deals with this every day may forget how dense it looks to you.
Legal and medical documents are often long because the law requires it.
A colleague may send everything at once because they are worried about leaving something out.
common_false_positives: A lease or loan agreement that is long because of legal requirements.
A hospital discharge sheet that covers a lot because the situation needs it.
A friend planning a wedding who messages you about ten details in one evening.
discernment_questions: Is the amount of material needed for this choice, or more than it needs?
When I ask for a summary or for more time, do I get it?
Could I explain the key terms back in my own words right now?
Would I agree to this if I had a week and a calm room?
Is the deadline real, and who set it?
less_concerning_if: A plain summary is available on request and matches the full text.
You can take the documents away and answer later without penalty.
Someone qualified, who has no stake in the outcome, can walk you through it.
more_concerning_if: The decision involves your home, income, health or legal rights.
You are told that asking for time will cost you the offer or the job.
The overload arrives alongside a deadline you cannot verify.
pattern_over_time_signs: You sign or agree to things you could not summarize afterwards.
You have begun to avoid opening their messages because of their length.
You feel stupid after most dealings with them, though you are not stupid in other areas.
Mistakes you were warned about in the fine print have cost you money or time.
Cognitive Overload.repair_check: Ask for the one-page version and see what comes back. Repair looks like a real summary, an honest answer about the parts that matter most, and an extension if you need one. A longer document or a sigh does not count as a change.
Cognitive Overload.boundary_respect_check: Say what you can manage: one question at a time, or the key terms on one page. Do they adapt? A person who respects the limit shortens the list. A person who does not will repeat the full load, or tell you everyone else coped.
Cognitive Overload.psychological_mechanism: Working memory is limited, and when it is full people tend to rely on shortcuts such as trusting whoever sounds confident or agreeing to finish. Stress and time pressure can reduce capacity further. Choosing the easiest path out can feel like a free choice in the moment, though it may be a response to overload.
Cognitive Overload.possible_impact_on_receiver: A fog, a sense of shutting down, and a signature given with vague unease are common accounts. Some feel ashamed that they did not understand, and so did not ask. Afterwards, some go through the documents and find terms they did not know they had accepted.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for a narrower version: 'This is a lot. Can you give me the three points that matter most, and I will read the rest tonight?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Refuse to decide in the pile: 'I am not going to sign something I have not read. I will take it home and give you an answer on Thursday.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop the meeting or call when you reach your limit: 'I have taken in all I can for today. Let's pick this up tomorrow.'
response_options.support_seeking: Have someone with no stake in the outcome read the documents with you, such as a legal aid clinic, a patient advocate or a trusted friend who reads closely.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask for a written summary of changes and priorities, and confirm back in writing which items you will do first and which will wait.

Cognitive Overload.boundary_script: "I want to understand this properly before I decide. Please send me the key terms on one page, and I will respond by Thursday afternoon."
Cognitive Overload.safety_note: Being overloaded is not itself a danger. It matters more where the decision touches your housing, income, health care or legal position, such as a lease, a benefits form or a settlement. For those, take time and ask a legal aid office, advocate or counselor to read it first. Never sign under pressure of time you cannot verify.
misuse_warning: Calling a genuinely complicated process 'overload' can lead you to distrust the people who are trying to explain it.
Using the label on a nervous over-explainer can punish someone who was trying to be careful.
Cognitive Overload.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Urgency Manufacturing shortens the clock; overload fills the time with so much material that the clock hardly matters. Interrogation demands answers from you, while overload pours material onto you. A False Dilemma shrinks your options to two, whereas overload buries them under detail so you cannot see how many options exist.

Bait and Switch.short_definition: Advertising or promising an appealing deal, then swapping in a worse one after the person is committed or has given something up.
Bait and Switch.core_meaning: Advertising or promising an appealing deal, then swapping in a worse one after the person is committed or has given something up.
Bait and Switch.expanded_definition: The bait is the attractive offer: a low price, a job title, a promised role, a shared plan. The switch comes once you have said yes, moved, paid a deposit or turned down alternatives, and the terms turn out to be different. Plans and prices change honestly, and an apology with a real fix is a different matter. It is a pattern when the better terms were never available, or the change always favors the person who made it.
Bait and Switch.plain_language_summary: You are drawn in by one offer, and after you commit, you are handed a worse one. By then, walking away costs more than going along.
Bait and Switch.why_this_matters: By the time the terms change, you have often given something up: a deposit, another offer, a move, a plan. Walking away costs more than accepting, and that cost is what makes a worse deal acceptable.
what_it_is: An offer made to attract you that was never going to be delivered in full.
A change in the terms that arrives after you have paid, moved, quit or declined something else.
Seen in ads and sales, job offers, rentals, services, and in personal promises.
The gap is explained as bad luck or 'things changed', though the change always benefits the one making it.
what_it_sounds_like: "That model just sold out, but I can offer you this one for a bit more."
"The role turned out to be different from what we discussed, but you'll grow into it."
"The price I gave you did not include the fees. Everyone pays them."
"I know I said we would live near your family, but this place makes more sense."
"The apartment is gone, but there is another one, slightly further out and pricier."
"That's not what I meant. You must have misunderstood."
what_it_is_not: A real change in circumstances that is explained openly and renegotiated fairly.
An honest error in a quote that the person corrects as soon as they notice, without leaning on you to accept it.
Terms that were clearly described as tentative or subject to approval at the time.
An item that actually sold out, where the seller truly has nothing else and says so.
Your own memory or hope shaping what was said. Writing things down is the only way to know.
this_may_be_it_when: The offer you were drawn in by was not available in the first place, or never would have been.
The change arrives only after you have committed, and not before.
The new terms favor them in every respect.
Your reminders of what was promised are met with 'that's not what I said'.
The same change has happened to other people dealing with them.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The change is explained, with documents, and you are free to walk away at no cost.
They offer a real remedy, such as refunding the deposit.
The terms moved in your favor as often as against.
The first offer was clearly marked as an estimate.
A third party, such as a supplier or an authority, truly changed the situation, and they told you promptly.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Stock, budgets and schedules do change, and honest people are sometimes forced to revise.
Someone may have overpromised out of enthusiasm and later face limits they had not foreseen.
A misunderstanding between two people can produce the same sense of a switch.
common_false_positives: A shop that really did run out of the advertised item and offers a rain check.
A job whose duties shifted when the company reorganized, and which was discussed openly.
A friend who planned a trip, then had to change it because of a family emergency.
discernment_questions: What exactly was promised, and do I have it in writing?
Did the change come before or after I committed?
Does the change benefit only them?
Would I have agreed if the current terms had been the first terms?
Am I being offered a fair way out, such as my money back?
less_concerning_if: They tell you about the change as soon as they know and offer a fair way out.
You can cancel with nothing lost.
The original offer was written down and they honor what they can.
more_concerning_if: You have given up housing, a job, a visa step or large sums before the switch.
They deny the original terms ever existed.
There is pressure to accept immediately or lose everything you have put in.
pattern_over_time_signs: You begin to keep screenshots and emails of what was said, because you expect it to change.
Each promise comes with a quiet exception that shows up later.
You are always the one adjusting to a new version of the deal.
You stop believing the first version of anything they say, and still feel unable to leave.
Bait and Switch.repair_check: Honest correction means the original terms are acknowledged, and you are offered a remedy that puts you back where you were, such as refund, release or the original deal. A new explanation that leaves you with the worse terms is not a fix, even when it comes with a warm apology.
Bait and Switch.boundary_respect_check: State the terms as you remember them and ask for a written confirmation. Does the person confirm, or argue about what was said? One who respects the limit puts it in writing and lets you decide.
Bait and Switch.psychological_mechanism: Once people have invested money, effort or hope, they tend to feel pulled to stay with the choice and to explain away discrepancies. A good first offer also anchors expectations, so the swapped version can seem like a small loss and not a different deal. Giving up other options makes walking away feel more costly.
Bait and Switch.possible_impact_on_receiver: Feeling foolish, cornered and unsure whether you misheard is a common account. Some are left out of pocket, or stuck in a job or home that is not what they chose. Some say the hardest part was that nothing could be proven, because the first offer had only been spoken.

response_options.soft_clarification: Restate it plainly: 'What I understood at the start was this price and this role. Has something changed that I should know about?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Insist on the original: 'I agreed to the first terms. I am not able to accept the new ones.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop adding to what you have already put in, such as more deposit, more time or more work, until the terms are confirmed in writing.
response_options.support_seeking: Show the original offer and the new one to someone neutral, such as a consumer advice office, a tenants' group or a friend who reads contracts.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask for the role, pay and duties in a signed letter before you start, and keep the original offer message. If terms shift, raise it in writing with HR.

Bait and Switch.boundary_script: "That is different from what we agreed at the start. I would like the original terms confirmed in writing today. If that cannot be done, I would like my deposit returned."
Bait and Switch.safety_note: Most switches cost money or time, but the stakes rise if the bait was housing, a job abroad, a visa-linked position or a loan. If you have moved, handed over documents, or owe money, keep records. Talk to a tenants' group, legal aid, a labor rights group or a consumer protection office before you accept new terms.
misuse_warning: Calling an honest change of plans 'bait and switch' can punish someone who told you promptly and offered a fair fix.
Using the term without checking what was actually promised can turn a misunderstanding into an accusation.
Bait and Switch.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Sunk Cost Exploitation uses what you have already invested to keep you in; the switch is the change in terms that triggers that pull. A False Dilemma gives you two options at the time of choosing, while here the choice was made on one set of terms and then changed. An Ultimatum attaches a penalty to a demand, whereas the switch simply alters what you agreed to.

Pre-Punishment.short_definition: Shutting yourself down before anyone else can, by not applying, speaking or trying, because past experience taught you that being seen gets punished.
Pre-Punishment.core_meaning: Shutting yourself down before anyone else can, by not applying, speaking or trying, because past experience taught you that being seen gets punished.
Pre-Punishment.expanded_definition: This is something a person does to themselves, so there may be no second party in the moment. After being mocked, shamed or hurt for standing out, a person can learn to remove the chance of being seen: skipping the application, staying silent in the meeting, never sending the draft. The punishment is imagined and delivered in advance. Caution is not the same thing. It becomes a pattern when it follows you into places where nothing like that has happened.
Pre-Punishment.plain_language_summary: You turn yourself down before anyone else gets the chance. You do not apply, speak or try, because it once felt dangerous to be noticed, and not trying feels safer.
Pre-Punishment.why_this_matters: Opportunities close before anyone else has the chance to refuse them. The cost, which includes jobs not applied for and things not said, stays invisible because nothing happened, and your life can narrow without anyone noticing.
what_it_is: Declining to try, apply, ask or speak based on a punishment you expect, not one that has happened.
A learned reflex: at some point, visibility was followed by ridicule, anger or loss, so staying small became a way to stay safe.
It can attach to success as well as failure, so that both feel unsafe.
Self-directed: the inner critic does the work that a critical person once did.
what_it_sounds_like: "There's no point applying. They would only laugh."
"If I speak up in the meeting, they will tear it apart."
"I'd rather not send it. Then no one can say it is bad."
"If I do well, they will expect more, and then I will be punished when I cannot keep it up."
Writing an email, rereading it eleven times and deleting it.
"Who do I think I am?" (in your own voice, before you have done anything)
what_it_is_not: A realistic judgment that the odds are poor, such as not applying for a job whose requirements you clearly do not meet.
Ordinary caution or humility, which needs no painful history behind it.
Choosing not to pursue something because of competing priorities, such as family, health or money.
Introversion or a preference for staying out of the spotlight, if it brings you no distress.
A needed rest. Pulling back during a hard season can be healthy.
this_may_be_it_when: You pull back from things you want, before anyone has said no.
The fear is specific: being noticed, laughed at, or held to a higher standard.
You can trace the reflex to an earlier place or person where standing out cost you.
The expected punishment is vivid, though you cannot point to anything like it happening in your present life.
Relief comes when you stay out of it, followed by quiet regret.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You have weighed the odds and honestly decided it is not for you.
You pass on things that do not interest you, and take up the ones that do.
Your caution fits a real risk in your present situation.
You turn down opportunities without distress, and do not later wish you had tried.
The pullback is brief, tied to a hard stretch, and lifts when your circumstances improve.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Nerves before a big step are ordinary, and most people feel them.
Tiredness, grief or illness can make everything look pointless for a while.
Some people simply prefer a quieter life and are content in it.
common_false_positives: Skipping a competition because you honestly do not enjoy competing.
Deciding not to apply for a role that would mean a long commute you cannot manage.
Shyness in new groups, which eases as you know people.
discernment_questions: What exactly do I expect to happen if I try, and has it ever happened to me?
Do I pull back from things I want, or things I do not care about?
When did I first learn that being seen was not safe?
Is there someone in my present life who would punish me, or only someone from my past?
If I imagined a kind friend in my place, what would I tell them to do?
less_concerning_if: You can name a clear, current reason for holding back that you are comfortable with.
You sometimes take the risk anyway, and it goes fine.
You do not feel regret afterwards.
more_concerning_if: Your life is shrinking: fewer applications, fewer friends, fewer words.
The fear is accompanied by hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm.
You still live or work with someone who does punish you for being visible.
pattern_over_time_signs: You keep a list of things you wanted to do and never did.
You watch others take chances you quietly wanted, and feel a pang.
Your reasons for not trying change, but the outcome never does.
You have begun to think of yourself as someone who is simply not made for opportunities.
Pre-Punishment.repair_check: Healing shows up in small, real tries: sending the application, speaking once in a meeting, and finding that the feared punishment did not come. Telling yourself it is time to be braver, without any actual try, leaves the reflex where it was.
Pre-Punishment.boundary_respect_check: Take one small step into view and notice the room. Does it respond the way you feared, or is the alarm mostly inside you while the room stays unmoved? That gap between expected and actual reaction is the useful fact.
Pre-Punishment.psychological_mechanism: If being visible was once followed by criticism or loss, the mind can learn to treat visibility as a threat. Avoiding the situation brings immediate relief, which tends to strengthen the avoidance. Because nothing bad happens when you do not try, the expectation is never tested.
Pre-Punishment.possible_impact_on_receiver: A quiet shrinking is the usual account: applications never sent, ideas never spoken, praise deflected. Some describe a tiredness from constant self-monitoring, and grief for what they did not try. Many say that seeing the reflex as old, and not as truth, was what first loosened it.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask yourself plainly: 'Who is the person I am afraid will react, and are they in this room?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Set a very small test: send one email or speak once this week, and write down what actually happened afterwards.
response_options.disengagement: When the inner critic starts its case, step away from the decision for a day and come back with a calmer eye.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a trusted person or a counselor about the old experience. Talking about when it began can loosen its hold.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Pick one low-stakes place to be visible, such as a short comment in a meeting, and ask a trusted colleague for plain feedback afterwards.

Pre-Punishment.boundary_script: "I notice I am talking myself out of this before anyone has said a word. That is an old habit, not today's facts. I am going to send the application and see what really happens."
Pre-Punishment.safety_note: Holding yourself back is a painful pattern but not by itself a danger. It deserves more care if it comes with hopelessness, thoughts of self-harm, or if you still live or work where being visible really is punished. In that case, talk to a counselor, a doctor or a crisis line, and think about what makes your present situation safe.
misuse_warning: Naming someone else's hesitation as 'pre-punishment' can dismiss a reasonable decision they made for sound reasons.
Treating all caution as an old wound can push a person to take risks that are not safe for them.
Pre-Punishment.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Ultimatums, False Dilemma and Interrogation all come from another person who presses on you. Pre-Punishment has no one pressing in the moment: the pressure is a remembered one, now carried inside. Sunk Cost Exploitation keeps you in something because of what you have already put in; pre-punishment keeps you out of things because of a punishment you expect.
